Copper Quarterly Report April 2010 

# Executive Summary Precarious balance 



- The copper market is in a delicate phase of the recovery, and our outlook is essentially unchanged from January.  The recovery in **consumption in the World ex-China** is coming through slightly earlier than we expected, but will still not regain the 2007-2008 peak within our forecast. **Chinese copper consumption** growth remains broad-based and mainly domestically generated.  We have slightly lowered 2010 Chinese growth compared to last time, but the earlier recovery in the World ex-China is more than offsetting any loss. 



- Prices of nearly $8,000/t face more downside than upside risk, but would have to fall by almost 50% to affect mine production plans.  Therefore, **mine project investment** is back on the agenda, particularly in concentrates projects given the tightness in availability.  The Chilean earthquake did not have a direct impact on production, so **refined production** continues with minimal disruptions.  We now expect that refined output in 2010 will be roughly level with that recorded in both 2008 and 2009, leading to a slight surplus this year, followed by a shift into a modest deficit next year. 



- **Scrap** availability is less of a problem than last year in the World ex-China.  However, in China scrap is tight, with imports still down 20% y-o-y in Q1 and changes in customs rules are likely to adversely affect imports following their implementation on 1<sup>st</sup> June.  Chinese scrap generation should grow, but not enough to fully offset the loss of imported material. 



- **Prices** have been supported by seasonally stronger demand and a gradual drawdown in LME stocks.  Rising SHFE stocks however leave total exchange stocks roughly unchanged since end-2009.  The investor support for LME prices continues, with the net effect of currency movements (weaker euro, potentially stronger renminbi) promoting short term volatility. 



- Sustained high prices and a return of risk appetite should see more mine projects proceed, but sustainable China-led consumption will mean that in the medium term we see the emergence of **larger deficits and rising prices** .

Chinese growth last year is 1.0% higher, but 2010 2.8% lower. Net global consumption last year is 110,000t higher and 2010 consumption is 45,000t greater. Consumption in the remaining years of the forecast has been raised by an average of 120,000tpy. The main driver is the earlier recovery in the World ex-China. **Supply** : Our refined production estimate for 2009 is 280,000t higher, due to disruptions being less than previously expected. Higher mine production and a lower disruption allowance has raised our forecast of refined production for 2010 by 400,000t, but our outlook in 2011-2014 is largely unchanged. **Prices** : Lowered by $500/t in 2010 and an average of $180/t in 2011-2014. ### Demand recovery and constrained supply sustain prices Market sentiment has been volatile, with positive news that the recovery in demand was proving fairly solid vying for attention with negative news about further financial trouble. The latter was driven mainly by the sovereign debt crisis in Europe, which saw the euro fall by over 7% against the dollar since mid-January. As a result, copper prices were equally volatility and traded in a wide $1,800/t range between January and mid-April. The fact that copper prices have held up in these conditions is supportive longer term. From a fundamental perspective, there was evidence of support for sustained high prices in Q1. Total inventory in LME warehouses had continued to climb through mid-February, but began to fall thereafter, as the demand for cathode picked up as the northern hemisphere ahead of the seasonally stronger consumption period in Q2. Most of the decline was in Asia, where LME stocks had begun to fall from January. Even US LME warehouses saw a slight decline in March. Unsurprisingly with copper prices hovering close to $7,500-$8,000/t, the copper industry was in a bullish mood at the recent CRU Copper Conference in Santiago, with most players optimistic on the outlook for copper demand and prices. Copper miners in particular are benefiting from higher copper prices. All of the majors were positive about mine project development, with Rio Tinto, Xstrata, Antofagasta and Anglo American all stating that they would be moving forward with their projects. Overall, the market is facing a precarious point in the recovery cycle. Demand is picking up but supply is more than holding its own thus far. We do not expect the economic recovery to be derailed. So we see supply continuing to struggle to keep pace with demand and expect the market to move into deficit next year. Our forecasts include a drawdown of some of the stocks that were built up in China last year. We estimate that the Chinese market recorded a 1.2Mt surplus in 2009, which accounts for virtually the entire global surplus. However, only 500,000700,000t of the build in stocks is likely to be surplus material that could be released to the market in the near term. We estimate that the other half of the 2009 stock build in China is held because of restocking, higher working stock requirements and the increase in SRB stocks. The risk is that the rate at which

surplus stocks are released to the Chinese market may be faster than the 100,000-200,000t we expect this year.  In this case imports would be lower and LME stocks would likely be higher, thus being a drag on prices. 

In addition to specific copper market factors, there are also several clouds on the horizon that could affect the high flying copper price.  Despite the financial crisis having led to an economic crisis, politicians have made only token efforts to reform the financial sector.  With successful financial reform needing to be coordinated internationally, US participation is vital.  Now that the marathon healthcare debate in the US has been won by President Obama, financial sector

reform is back on the political agenda in the US and elsewhere.  How financial market reform will affect the commodity markets is unclear and will remain so until proposals are more concrete.  One thing is certain however: exchange rates will remain volatile and drive volatility in copper prices.  Financial crises are usually followed by sovereign defaults, so we also expect more ructions in international bond markets, though whether this translates into a resumption of wider financial market stress is an unknown quantity at the moment.  Overall, we believe that the risks of downside exposure likely outweigh those on the upside.  In addition, barring any catastrophe that reduces supply significantly, the scope for the decline in prices is greater than the potential upside. 

### Demand recovery accelerates in World ex-China… 

The recovery in demand in the World ex-China is proving to be stronger than we anticipated in the previous Quarterly.  The main contributors are Japan and Russia, which together saw a stronger H2 2009 bounce back in consumption from the lows plumbed in H1 last year.  With Q1 2010 also looking stronger, Japanese consumption is now forecast to be over 100,000t higher than we had forecast in the January Quarterly and Russia 85,000t higher this year. 

The Japanese renaissance was particularly strong at the brass mills, which experienced a rapid recovery during the last few months of 2009 that has carried forward into the first quarter of 2010.  Our latest estimate shows that Japanese copper flat rolled product output increased 66.5% y-o-y in Q1 2010 and in Korea total semis production is above the pre-crisis level.  The recovery in Russia has been better than we expected.  In particular, wirerod production has not suffered as much as we had expected following the change in the tariffs that had previously favoured exporting wirerod instead of cathode.  Russian wirerod output fell by “only” 39% last year instead of the 47% we had previously estimated.

Overall, we now estimate that consumption in the World ex-China fell by less than we previously estimated and we have also raised the forecast growth rate for 2010 to 5.5% from 4.7%. With the upward revisions in Japanese and Russian consumption forecasts and slight upward revisions elsewhere, total World ex-China consumption in 2010 is now forecast to be 150,000t higher than presented in the January Quarterly. ### …and China still strong Chinese refined consumption growth has been revised up to 22.5% in 2009, representing a 1.1Mt increase in consumption compared to 2008. The twin drivers of this were the sharp recovery in semis production, up an estimated 14%, combined with the shar

p decline in global scrap availability that resulted in a boost to refined consumption of 500,000t.  The shortfall in scrap will persist in 2010, however we estimate that a run down in copper scrap stocks and higher domestic scrap generation following the success of the household appliance scrappage schemes means that the shortfall will amount to only 100,000-150,000t this year.  Thus, we now expect total refined consumption will be will be up by 12% in 2010, slightly faster than our forecast of a 10% increase in GDP. 

However, the government’s announcement of plausible RMB appreciation has raised concern among industry participants, particularly those with export businesses whose margins would be squeezed by lower export earnings in renminbi terms or a loss of market share due to having to raise prices.  However, the opposite effect of lower cathode prices for Chinese fabricators would be limited, as LME prices would be bid up to reflect the changes in currency values, thus offsetting the currency effect.  In fact, the revaluation could be taken by investors as a vote of confidence by the Chinese government in the strength of the economy and therefore demand for commodities including copper, which could cause even higher levels of investor activity in commodity markets, including copper.

### Production continues to surprise on the upside… 

Once again, production in 2009 came in higher than expected, as the “usual” disruptions were conspicuous by their absence.  There were a few new labour related disruptions and those that occurred over the past three months were short-lived, such as a brief stoppage at Ok Tedi in Papua New Guinea.  We now estimate the mine production last year grew by 1.7%; our EW production estimate is all but unchanged but concentrates output is now estimated to have risen by 1.3%.  However, electro-refined copper output in 2009 fell by 0.4%, to just over 18Mt, due to smelter cutbacks and constraints on availability of high grade scrap used at the anode casting stage. 

The overriding factor affecting smelting and refining production over the next five years will be the availability of raw materials, chiefly concentrates but also scrap.  The concentrates market has been in deficit for the last four years and the imbalance between mine supply and smelters’ requirements is expected to persist.  Indeed the shortfall in concentrate availability is expected to rise over the next four years, as the growth in smelter capacity will outstrip that of mine production.  Improved by-product revenues as acid and precious metals prices continue to rise mean that long term contract TC/RCs are now covering smelter operating costs in Japan and Europe as well as China.  However, current spot TC/RCs are well below breakeven levels. 

Smelting rationalisation continues, with Grupo Mexico announcing that it will close its San Luis Potosi smelt

er in 2010. No reason has been given, but the smelter has only been producing 20,000t/y of blister copper, well below its nominal capacity of 50,000t/y. Therefore, the impact of this closure on global concentrate availability will be even less than that of Xstrata’s closure of Kidd Creek. The refined metal market continues to improve and acid storage capacity is no longer a restriction. Therefore, there have been no new smelter cutbacks announced, though some remain in place in Japan, Europe and Kazakhstan. production, with all Japanese smelters except PPC announcing higher y-o-y output plans for the 2010-11 fiscal year that began 1st April. With producers looking to reverse cutbacks and

capacity continuing to rise in China, pressure on already tight concentrates availability will increase over the next five years.  We also anticipate that scrap availability will fall short of requirements as new Chinese secondary capacity is set to increase.  Therefore, further cutbacks at existing operations or delays to projects will be required.  We are now forecasting that raw materials (both concentrate and scrap) will fall short of smelter demand by over 2Mt contained copper by 2012, peaking at 2.3Mt in 2013, and production will need to be adjusted as a result. The average rate of capacity utilisation will fall to just 65% in 2012, if there are no further rationalisations.  In addition, availability of high grade scrap for anode production is also expected to fall short of requirements, requiring further cutbacks of some 450,000t by 2012. 

With cutbacks and/or closures necessary, the question facing the concentrates and scrap markets is which are the most vulnerable smelters?  The two key factors to be considered are the financial position of an operation and security of raw material supply.  However, product marketing and government or fiscal support may also have an influence.  The Japanese smelters have the highest operating costs and less favourable payment terms for by-product precious metals than their European counterparts.  However, they are unlikely to close as they are part of large conglomerates and are investing abroad to secure concentrate feed.  Other smelters though are vulnerable to closures, particularly including: 

- Custom smelters, facing low TC/RCs and shortages in supply. 

- Small and/or less environmentally sound smelters. 



- Chinese smelters that are dependent on the spot market either directly or via traders for a significant proportion of their concentrate requirements.  This will make them more vulnerable to shortfalls in availability.

Adjustm|ent for|| - Those Chinese smelters and refineries with a higher dependency on scrap are also expected to be hit more heavily by the insufficient availability of scrap. #### BUT - The industry in China will receive national and provincial government support, meaning they will likely continue to operate at lower utilisation rates than smelters elsewhere. ### …with project development back on the agenda Despite the positive mood, delays to mine projects continue, with banks still reluctant to finance major projects, particularly in countries with a high risk profile. The credit crunch has also resulted in delays to a number of major projects as development was slowed down or halted in 2009. The strong growth in refined copper demand and high prices that we are forecasting will encourage producers to accelerate project development where possible and we have raised the probability factors for our committed, probable and possible projects. The tight concentrates market and low treatment charges will provide an additional incentive to bring on concentrates projects, particularly where smelters have an ownership share. Delays to planned copper projects though remain a constant threat to our forecasts. Experience over the past few years suggests that the extent of production disruptions have been consistently underestimated and, as the hurdles to developing new mines grow higher, delays to new capacity are ever present. Moreover, since the global financial crisis, risk appetite has changed with the small to medium sized producers struggling to find financing as easily. ### Balance shifts towards deficits, beginning next year Following flat refined production for the past two years, we forecast increases averaging almost 5% per year over the period 2011-2014. A number of major projects could potentially come on CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly Report April 2010 Executive Summary 9 stream in 2012-2014. In the near term, brownfield projects and restarts will contribute the bulk of new copper supply entering the market. By 2013, we expect g

reenfield projects to supply over 50% of new production, and in 2014, this is set to become more pronounced as a number of major new developments come on-stream. 

Smelters, on the other hand continue to face difficult operating conditions.  They see only a limited benefit from the higher copper price and are facing a growing shortfall in the availability of raw materials for smelting.  Strong growth in copper demand in China continues to encourage investment in new smelting and refining capacity as the country aims to be self sufficient in both refined copper and semis production.  China remains the driving force of consumption, both to meet the requirements of its own domestic end-use demand but also as it becomes the powerhouse of semis capacity as well as the provider of both semis and final products for export.  However, the world ex-China will not stand still and we forecast relatively robust demand growth as it recovers from the depths of the 2009 recession, leading to global growth averaging 5.5% over the 2011to 2014 period. 

At the same time we forecast that total refined copper production will grow at an annual average rate of almost 5% between 2011 and 2014, fuelled in part by delays to projects as a result of the global financial crisis.  However, the rate will slow from over 5% in 2012 and 2013 to below 4% in 2014.  As demand growth outstrips that of supply in the refined market and the build up in exchange inventories begun to be  eroded, copper prices will recover robustly. 

The annual deficits we estimate are small compared to the underlying totals of around 20Mtpy.  Modest deficits in the earlier years of our forecast, 2011 to 2013, will keep prices above $3.30/lb ($7,275/t).  By 2014, however, as the stock to consumption ratio dwindles to precariously low levels, we expect to see prices target levels above $3.75/lb ($8,250/t). 

### Points to watch 

#### **Downside** 



- The main downside risk is a macroeconomic shock, such as another financial sector meltdown in the developed world or China slamming on the economic brakes too strongly. 



- Investors could see more potential upside in the global manufacturing sector during a new upswing.  If copper looks less attractive relative to other alternatives, they could become net sellers. 



- The remedies in the US anti-dumping case that will be decided in May could be more severe than anticipated and cause a short term dip in prices as the news is assimilated by the market. 



- Economisation and substitution –the record gap between copper prices and those of competing materials (especially aluminium) is not going to go away and will lead to a return of the substitution threat. 



- Automotive: scrappage schemes have only brought forward demand from future quarters threatening another mini-boom/bust cycle in 2010 as schemes are unwound. 

- Construction: Lack of credit growth threatens an extended period of weak growth. 



- Should any of the above lead to prices falling,

we anticipate the SRB would come back into the market to continue replenishing stocks, thus limiting the downside to any price correction.

#### **Upside** 









- Chinese control of macroeconomic policy could be insufficient and the momentum built up in 2009 could see a spike in imports and the copper price in the short term, though this would likely be followed by a bust once the brakes are applied more vigorously. 

- Industrialised world could see an earlier economic recovery than forecast, which would see more rapid re-stocking and a jump in the price. 

- Mine underperformance will generally provide support for prices.  Beyond 2010, a return of production growth threatens a return of high capital cost inflation (as during the boom years), as miners scramble to obtain equipment to expand operations. 

- There is continued upside price potential if investors choose to view copper as part of a longterm commodities as an asset class play.
